title: Prose / Bullet Mix — and No Repetition Between Them
description: A TR doc must MIX short paragraphs with bullets. Added after the reviewer's note that 'mostly all the content is bullets only, which looks odd' — and it did, because every earlier rule pushed the same way ('prefer bullets/tables over text'), so even pairs of short related points came back as lists. Two countable halves: at least 60% of slides must carry a `text` block (a short framing paragraph of <= 55 words / 2-3 sentences saying what the slide is about), and no bullet list may have fewer than 3 items, since a one- or two-item list is a sentence somebody bulleted. Bullets stay for genuine lists of 3+ parallel, substantial items; tables stay for any 2+ way comparison. SECOND HALF, added after the reviewer found it on nearly every slide: the paragraph and the bullets beneath it must carry DIFFERENT information. A lead-in sentence followed by bullets that restate it in other words is the costliest defect on a slide — the page ceiling is fixed, so every repeated line is a line that cannot teach something new ('if you are repeating content, we will cover less information only'). The division of labour: the paragraph frames (what this is, why it exists, how it relates), the bullets carry the specifics it does not state (steps, types, values, conditions, trade-offs, where it is used). Apply the deletion test — if deleting the paragraph loses nothing, or deleting the bullets loses nothing, the slide says one thing twice. A guardrail fails a bullet whose distinctive words are >= 50% already in the paragraph; paraphrase that shares no vocabulary is the judge's half of this set.
criterion: >= 60% of slides contain a `text` block; every bullet list has >= 3 items; and no bullet restates the paragraph above it, in any wording.

rubric.5: Mix is right and every line on a slide adds something no other line gave.
rubric.3: One of the three breached on a slide or two.
rubric.1: Wall-to-wall bullets, bulleted one/two-item 'lists', or bullets that are the lead-in sentence again.

content.text: SCTP carries several independent streams inside one association, so a loss on one stream does not stall the others.

items: Each stream keeps its own sequence space
Loss blocks only the affected stream

cases.rationale: A framing paragraph, then a real 3-item list — the intended shape.
No framing paragraph, and a 2-item 'list' that is really one sentence.

input.doc_shape: 12 slides, 2 of which carry a `text` block

cases.rationale: 17% of slides carry prose — under the 60% floor; this is the wall of bullets the reviewer rejected.

content.text: Interrupt-driven I/O still burdens the CPU with copying each byte; DMA lets a dedicated controller transfer data directly.

items: DMA controller moves data memory-to-device directly
CPU only sets up transfer, then continues
Single interrupt signals whole block completion

cases.rationale: Bullets 1 and 4 are the two halves of the sentence restated; only bullets 2 and 3 add anything. Four lines of a fixed page budget, two lines of new information.

content.text: Applications call generic read, write and control operations; device drivers translate these into device-specific commands.

items: System calls expose a uniform I/O interface
Device drivers hide hardware-specific command details
Same read/write call works across device types

cases.rationale: All three bullets paraphrase the sentence — the slide teaches one idea and spends four lines on it. The learner ends knowing no more than the first sentence gave.

content.text: Interrupt-driven I/O makes the processor copy every byte itself, which collapses at disk speeds. DMA hands that work to a dedicated controller.

items: Setup: CPU writes source, destination and count registers
Transfer: controller drives the bus while the CPU works
Completion: one interrupt per block, not per byte
Cost: cycle stealing contends for bus bandwidth
Used by disk, network and audio streaming

cases.rationale: The rewrite of mix-bad-3: the paragraph frames the problem, and the bullets carry the mechanism, its cost and where it is used — none of it in the paragraph. Delete either and something is lost.
